label: Lead
summary: Lead in old solder, CRT glass, old paint, batteries, wheel weights and old pipes is toxic. It builds up in the body and damages nerves, kidneys and the brain. Children and pregnant women are harmed most, at doses that cause no symptoms.
signs: Dull grey solder on older circuit boards
Lead-acid batteries and the crust around them
Flaking or chalky old paint, especially in buildings from before the 1980s
Wheel weights, fishing weights, old pipes and roof flashing
do: Wash hands and face before eating, drinking or smoking
Work outdoors or with a through-draught
Wet old paint before scraping it
Change clothes after dirty work and wash them separately
Keep children and pregnant women away from lead work and lead dust
dont: Don't sand, grind or burn old paint
Don't melt lead indoors or anywhere near food
Don't eat, drink or smoke while working with lead
Don't keep food or water in lead-soldered or lead-glazed containers
Don't dry-sweep or blow lead dust: wipe it up with wet rags or a wet mop
Don't let water, damp scrap or a wet mould touch molten lead: it turns to steam and throws molten metal
ppe: A P100 (P3) respirator for dust and fumes
Work clothes you leave at the door
firstAid: There is no quick fix: stop the exposure and keep it stopped
Stomach pain, headaches, tiredness, irritability, or a child falling behind after exposure needs medical attention
Only a blood test confirms lead poisoning
A child who swallowed a lead weight, pellet or paint chips needs medical care quickly: lead dissolves in the stomach
